steps: Step 1, Sit and set up: Amina sits with both feet on the floor, the screen at eye level, and one hand on the mouse. She finds the pointer arrow on the screen and moves the mouse slowly until the arrow touches the big green square.

Step 2, Click: With the arrow on the green square, Amina presses the left button once and lets go. The square turns yellow. One quick press is a click. She says 'click' aloud each time to remember the single press.

Step 3, Drag: Amina puts the arrow on a red ball, holds the left button down, slides the mouse to the basket on the right, then lets go. The ball drops into the basket. Hold, move, release is called dragging.

Step 4, Find letters: Her teacher shows a box and the letters A, M, I, N. Amina looks at the keyboard, finds the A key on the left side of the middle row, and presses it once. An 'a' appears in the box.

Step 5, Type the name: She types A, then holds the Shift key with her little finger while pressing A for a capital, so the first letter is right. Next come m, i, n, a. The screen shows Amina, five letters.

Step 6, Check and fix: She reads the screen letter by letter, touching each one with the pointer: A-m-i-n-a. All five match. If a letter were wrong she would press Backspace once to remove the last letter and type again.

Your turn: Your name is Omar. Click the blue button, drag a star into a box, then type your name with a capital O. Model answer: O comes from Shift plus the O key, then m, a, r. The screen shows Omar, four letters, and the star sits inside the box.
Step 1, Open the tool: Lina clicks the drawing tool icon, a paintbrush on the desktop. A white page opens with a row of colour squares at the top and a pencil, a brush and an eraser on the left side.

Step 2, Pick a colour and tool: She clicks the yellow square, then the brush. The pointer changes to a small dot. Yellow is now the colour she will draw with, so everything she paints from here will be yellow.

Step 3, Draw the sun: Holding the left button down, Lina moves the mouse in a slow circle in the top corner. When the circle joins up she lets go. A yellow round sun appears. She adds five short lines around it for rays.

Step 4, Change colour for the house: She clicks the red square and draws a square box in the middle of the page for the house wall. Then she clicks brown and draws a triangle on top for the roof, making a simple house.

Step 5, Fix a mistake: One ray crossed the roof. Lina clicks the eraser tool, rubs over only that crossing line, and the white page shows again. She switches back to the yellow brush and draws the ray shorter.

Step 6, Save: Lina clicks the save button, types the name 'my house' and presses Enter. The tool shows 'my house' at the top. She now has a picture with a sun, a house and a roof that she can open tomorrow.

Your turn: Draw a tree with a brown trunk and a green top, then erase one mistake and save it as 'tree'. Model answer: pick brown and draw a thin tall rectangle, pick green and draw a round top, use the eraser on any stray mark, then save with the name tree.
Step 1, The situation: At break, Zaid has two biscuits. Maryam sits next to him and has none because she forgot her lunch box. Zaid notices she is looking at the floor and is very quiet.

Step 2, Notice feelings: Zaid asks himself, 'How does Maryam feel?' Her shoulders are down and she is not talking, so he thinks she is sad and hungry. Noticing how someone feels is the first step of kindness.

Step 3, Choices: Zaid sees three choices. He can eat both biscuits, eat one and hide the other, or give one to Maryam. He thinks about how each choice would make Maryam feel and how it would make him feel.
Step 4, The kind choice: Zaid says, 'Maryam, would you like one of my biscuits?' She smiles and says, 'Thank you!' He now has one biscuit and she has one. Two children are eating, not one.

Step 5, Why it matters: Zaid still has one biscuit, so he lost only a little. Maryam gained a lot, because she was hungry. Sharing makes both children feel warm, and Maryam may share with someone else another day.

Step 6, Say it: Zaid finishes the sentence, 'It is kind to share because it helps a friend who needs it.' Kind actions are things you do, like giving or helping, plus kind words like please and thank you.

Your turn: Sara has one pencil and Hamdan has none during writing time. What can Sara do and why? Model answer: Sara can lend the pencil first or share by taking turns, because Hamdan needs it now and sharing helps him write and feel included.

Step 1, Open the editor: Hind clicks the Start button, finds the text editor in the list, and clicks it once. A white empty page opens with a blinking line at the top left. That blinking line is the cursor.

Step 2, Type a sentence: She clicks inside the page and types 'My cat is called Noor.' She presses the Space bar between words and the full stop key at the end. Five words and a full stop appear on one line.
Step 3, New line: Hind presses Enter. The cursor jumps to the next line. She types 'Noor likes milk.' Now the page has two lines, each starting with a capital letter and ending with a full stop.
Step 4, Fix a typing mistake: She sees 'mlik' instead of 'milk'. She clicks just after the k, presses Backspace four times to delete all of 'mlik', and types milk again. The word now reads correctly.

Step 5, Save and name: Hind presses Ctrl and S together. A box asks for a name. She types 'my-cat' and presses Enter. The title at the top of the window changes to my-cat, which means the file is saved.

Step 6, Close and reopen: She closes the editor, then opens the Documents folder and double-clicks my-cat. Both lines come back unchanged, which proves the file was saved. Choosing a clear name made it easy to find.

Your turn: Type 'I like apples.' on line one and 'They are red.' on line two, then save it as 'apples'. Model answer: Ctrl+S, type apples, Enter. Reopening apples shows two lines, each with a capital letter and a full stop.

Step 1, Choose a shape: Yusuf opens the drawing tool and clicks the rectangle shape in the tool list. He drags from the left of the page to the middle, down and across, and lets go. A square outline appears for a house wall.

Step 2, Fill with colour: He clicks the fill tool, which looks like a paint bucket, picks orange, and clicks inside the rectangle. The whole wall turns orange. The bucket fills only inside closed lines, so the outline must have no gaps.

Step 3, Add a triangle roof: Yusuf selects the triangle shape, drags a triangle on top of the wall, then fills it brown with the bucket. The page now shows an orange wall and a brown roof, which is two shapes.
Step 4, Add a circle window: He selects the circle shape and holds Shift while dragging so the circle is round. He puts it on the wall and fills it light blue. Now the house has one round window.

Step 5, Undo: Yusuf accidentally fills the sky area black with the bucket. He presses Ctrl and Z once. The black disappears and the page returns to the step before. Undo cancels only the last action each time.
Step 6, Count and save: The finished picture has 3 shapes, a rectangle, a triangle and a circle, filled in 3 colours. Yusuf presses Ctrl and S, names it 'my house', and presses Enter to keep it.

Your turn: Make a boat from a rectangle hull and a triangle sail, fill both, undo one mistake. Model answer: draw the rectangle, fill brown; draw a triangle above it, fill white; if a wrong fill happens press Ctrl+Z once. Two shapes, two colours.
Step 1, The problem: Laila and Dana are friends. At playtime both want the same red scooter. Laila grabs it first, Dana frowns and says, 'You always get it,' and walks away looking upset.

Step 2, Name the feelings: Laila notices Dana is sad and a little cross. Laila feels bad too, because she wants her friend. Naming feelings, 'I am sad, she is cross,' helps both children calm down before talking.
Step 3, Choices: Laila could ride away and ignore Dana, say 'It is mine,' or fix the problem. She thinks of two kind fixes, taking turns or finding another game they can do together.
Step 4, Kind words: Laila walks over and says, 'Sorry I grabbed it. Let's take turns. I go to the wall, then you go.' Her words say sorry, give an idea, and use a calm voice with no shouting.
Step 5, Result: Dana says, 'Okay, you first, then me.' Laila rides to the wall and back, gives Dana the scooter, and Dana rides. Both children had a turn, and the friendship is safe.
Step 6, Why it worked: Laila said sorry, used a fair idea, and listened. A small problem does not need to end a friendship if each child shows care. Friends solve problems kindly, not by winning.

Your turn: Two friends both want the last green crayon. What should they do and say? Model answer: one says, 'Can we take turns? You use it first for two minutes, then I do.' Both agree, share the crayon kindly, and stay friends.

Step 1, The job: Karim agrees to be the plant helper for his class. His job is to water the two class plants every Monday and Thursday before the first lesson. Having a clear job with clear days makes it simple.
Step 2, Make a reminder: Karim draws a small chart with two rows, Monday and Thursday, and a tick box beside each. He puts the chart near the door where he can see it as he comes in each morning.
Step 3, Do the job: On Monday he fills the small jug with water, gives each plant one jug, wipes a drop from the table, and ticks the Monday box. The plants are watered and the table is clean.
Step 4, A hard day: On Thursday Karim forgets until lunch. He does not hide it. He tells his teacher, 'I forgot the plants.' He waters them straight away and ticks the box with a note, 'late'.

Step 5, Why honesty matters: Being responsible does not mean never forgetting. It means doing what you promised, owning a mistake, and fixing it quickly. The plants are fine, and his teacher trusts him because he told the truth.
Step 6, Count the result: In one week Karim did 2 of 2 jobs, one on time and one late. Next week he moves the chart to his bag so he sees it on both days. Fixing the system helps him remember.

Your turn: You must feed the home pet every evening. Make a plan for one week and say what to do if you forget. Model answer: tick chart on the fridge, feed at 6 pm, and if you forget, tell an adult at once and feed it now.
Step 1, The game: Four children, Bilal, Aisha, Sami and Rana, want to use one slide at the same time in the playground. Everybody pushes toward the ladder, and Sami almost falls.
Step 2, What goes wrong: With no rule, the biggest or fastest child wins and the others get hurt or left out. Aisha says, 'This is not fair and it is not safe.' The children agree they need a rule.

Step 3, Make a rule: Rana suggests, 'We line up in a row, and each person goes down once, then goes to the back.' The line gives the order: Bilal, Aisha, Sami, Rana. Everyone understands who goes next.
Step 4, Take turns: Bilal slides first and walks to the back. Aisha goes second, Sami third, Rana fourth. After four slides each child has had exactly one turn, so the count is equal at one each.

Step 5, A child breaks the rule: Sami tries to go twice in a row. Aisha says calmly, 'It is Rana's turn, then you.' Sami goes to the back and waits. The rule is the same for every child, so it is fair.

Step 6, Explain it: Rules help because they keep us safe, give everyone a turn and stop arguments. The slide rule works for the big child and the small child in the same way, and that is what fairness means.

Your turn: Three children share two scooters at break. Make a fair rule. Model answer: two ride for three minutes while one waits, then the waiting child swaps with one rider. Over three turns each child rides twice and waits once.

Step 1, Insert a shape: Farah opens the drawing program, selects the arrow shape from the shapes menu, and drags to draw an arrow pointing right on the page. The arrow has small square handles at its corners and edges.

Step 2, Resize: She drags the bottom right corner handle outward and the arrow grows bigger while keeping its proportions. Dragging a corner handle changes both width and height together, so the shape does not get squashed.

Step 3, Rotate: She grabs the round rotate handle above the shape and turns it a quarter turn clockwise. The arrow, which pointed right, now points down. She also uses the menu Rotate right 90 degrees and gets the same result.

Step 4, Colour: With the arrow still selected, Farah picks Fill, chooses green and sets the outline to dark blue. The arrow becomes green with a blue edge. Selecting before colouring is important, or nothing changes.
Step 5, Copy and check: She copies the arrow with Ctrl+C, pastes with Ctrl+V, and rotates the copy 180 degrees. Now one arrow points down and one points up, each green with a blue edge.
Step 6, Save: Farah chooses File, Save as, types 'arrows', picks the picture format PNG, and presses Save. The file arrows.png appears in the folder. She reopens it and sees both arrows unchanged.

Your turn: Draw a triangle, make it twice as large, rotate it 90 degrees to the left, colour it red, and save it as 'tri'. Model answer: drag a corner handle to double its size, rotate left 90, fill red, then Save as tri.png.

Step 1, Posture and home row: Sultan sits straight with wrists level. His left fingers rest on A, S, D, F and his right fingers on J, K, L and the semicolon key. Thumbs rest on the Space bar. This is the home row.

Step 2, Type a short text: He opens the word processor and types 'The desert is hot in summer.' Then he presses Enter and types 'Camels can walk far without any water.' That is two sentences, 13 words in total.

Step 3, Check the count: Sultan counts: sentence one has 6 words, sentence two has 7 words. 6 plus 7 is 13. The word count shown at the bottom of the program also says 13, so his typing and counting match.

Step 4, Format the title: He adds a line at the top, 'Desert Facts', selects it by dragging, then clicks Bold, sets the size from 12 to 18, and clicks Centre. The title is now large, bold and in the middle.

Step 5, Format the body: He selects the two sentences and changes the font to a clear one, keeps the size at 12, and clicks Align left. Small, clear text for the body and large text for the title looks neat.
Step 6, Save: Sultan presses Ctrl+S, names the file 'desert-facts' and presses Enter. He closes and reopens it, and the bold centred title and two sentences are still there.

Your turn: Type a title 'My School' and two sentences about it, make the title bold and centred, size 16. Model answer: title is selected, Bold, Centre, size 16 from the size box; body stays at 12; save as my-school.
Step 1, Pick a need: Hessa's class notices the school cleaner works hard, and the plant pots at the school door are dry. Hessa asks, 'What small act of service could we do for our school this week?'

Step 2, Choose one act: The class lists three ideas: write thank-you cards to the cleaner, water the plants, or pick up litter on the field. They vote by raising hands: 12 for cards, 8 for plants, 6 for litter. Cards win.

Step 3, Plan the act: Hessa writes the plan. Who: all 26 children. What: one thank-you card each. When: Tuesday morning. Materials: paper and crayons. Check: 12 plus 8 plus 6 is 26 votes, so every child voted once.

Step 4, Split jobs: Each child writes 'Thank you for keeping our school clean' plus their name and a drawing. Hessa gives out paper, Ali collects the cards in a box, and the teacher helps tie them with a ribbon.
Step 5, Do it: On Tuesday the class gives the box of 26 cards to the cleaner. She smiles and says, 'This makes my day.' Nobody asked for a reward, because the act was given freely and kindly.
Step 6, Reflect: Hessa says, 'We helped one person feel noticed. It cost no money and took ten minutes.' Next week the class plans the plant watering. A small planned act can happen again and again.

Your turn: Plan a small act of service for a neighbour or the school library. Model answer: act is tidying library books on Wednesday; who is four children, jobs are sort, stack, label; check that all books return to the right shelf.
Step 1, The task: Group of four, Omar, Dina, Hamad and Sana, must build a poster about water saving in 30 minutes. The poster has four parts: title, a picture, three tips and colouring.

Step 2, Share jobs fairly: They list the jobs and match strengths. Omar writes the title, Dina draws the picture, Hamad writes the three tips, and Sana does the colouring. Four jobs, four children, one job each.
Step 3, Check time: The group plans time. Title 5 minutes, picture 10, tips 10, colouring 5. Total is 5 plus 10 plus 10 plus 5, which is 30 minutes. The plan fits exactly the time they have.

Step 4, A problem: Hamad finishes his tips in 6 minutes, not 10. Dina has not finished drawing. Hamad says, 'I am done, can I help?' Dina says yes and he draws the water drops, so the picture finishes on time.

Step 5, Listening: When Sana wants a blue border and Omar prefers green, they listen to each other and vote with Dina and Hamad. Three of four choose blue. Omar accepts the result politely and helps colour.

Step 6, Result and reflection: The poster is done in 28 minutes, with the whole group's names on it. They say, 'We shared jobs, helped each other and listened.' Teamwork meant nobody did everything and nobody did nothing.

Your turn: A team of three must make a model of a mosque from boxes in 20 minutes. Assign jobs and time. Model answer: Child A cuts boxes 8 minutes, B glues 8 minutes, C paints 4 minutes; 8+8+4=20; whoever finishes early helps another.

Step 1, Plan three slides: Mariam must present 'Our Local Birds' in about two minutes. She plans 3 slides: slide 1 the title, slide 2 'Falcon' with one picture and two short points, slide 3 'Flamingo' laid out the same way.

Step 2, Title slide: She opens the slide tool, picks the Title layout, clicks the top box and types 'Our Local Birds', then clicks the lower box and types 'By Mariam, Grade 4'. The first slide now has a title and a name.

Step 3, Add a slide with text: She clicks New Slide, picks Title and Content, types 'Falcon' as the heading, then two bullets: 'Fast flyer' and 'Hunts small animals'. Each bullet has about three words, so the audience reads quickly.

Step 4, Insert a picture: On slide 2 she clicks Insert, then Picture, chooses her own drawing 'falcon.png' from the Pictures folder, and drags a corner handle to resize it so it sits at the right without covering the bullets.

Step 5, Copy the layout: She duplicates slide 2 to make slide 3, changes the heading to 'Flamingo', the bullets to 'Pink feathers' and 'Stands on one leg', and replaces the picture with flamingo.png. The deck has 3 slides.

Step 6, Practise and save: In slideshow mode she presses the right arrow key twice to move through slides 1, 2 and 3, reading each in about 30 seconds, then saves as 'local-birds'. Total talk time is 3 slides at 30 seconds, 90 seconds.

Your turn: Make a 3-slide talk on 'My Favourite Food' with one picture. Model answer: slide 1 title and name; slide 2 a food heading, two short bullets and one picture; slide 3 another food or a summary with a picture; save and practise.
Step 1, Goal: Tariq wants a sprite to draw a square on the stage using a block-coding tool. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. He plans to repeat one move and one turn four times.
Step 2, Start event: From the Events category he drags 'when green flag clicked' to the coding area. An event block starts the program only when the flag is clicked, so nothing happens until then.
Step 3, Pen and loop: Under it he snaps 'pen down' and then a 'repeat 4' block. Inside the repeat he snaps 'move 100 steps' and 'turn right 90 degrees'. Four times: move, turn.
Step 4, Predict: The sprite moves 100, turns 90, moves 100, turns 90, moves 100, turns 90, moves 100, turns 90. Total turning is 4 times 90, which is 360 degrees, so it ends facing the way it began.

Step 5, Run and check: Tariq clicks the green flag. A square with sides of 100 steps is drawn and the sprite ends where it began. If he forgets pen down, the sprite moves but leaves no line, so he checks that block first.

Step 6, Add a second event: He adds 'when space key pressed' then 'say Done! for 2 seconds'. Pressing the space bar makes a speech bubble show Done! for 2 seconds. Two events, two separate small programs.

Your turn: Draw a triangle with sides of 100. Model answer: when green flag clicked, pen down, repeat 3, move 100 steps, turn right 120 degrees. 3 times 120 is 360, so the sprite finishes facing its starting direction.
Step 1, Enter data: Sara surveys 22 classmates about pets. In a spreadsheet she types Pet in A1 and Number in B1, then Cat 6, Dog 9, Fish 4, Bird 3 in rows 2 to 5. Each fact goes in its own cell.
Step 2, Check the total: She clicks cell B6 and types =SUM(B2:B5) then Enter. The spreadsheet shows 22. By hand, 6 plus 9 is 15, 15 plus 4 is 19, 19 plus 3 is 22, so the formula and the survey agree.
Step 3, Select for the chart: She drags from A1 to B5 to select the labels and the numbers, but not the total row. Including the total would draw a fifth tall bar and mislead readers.
Step 4, Insert chart: She clicks Insert, then Chart, and chooses a column chart. Four bars appear: Cat reaches 6, Dog 9, Fish 4, Bird 3. A column chart is good for comparing separate groups.
Step 5, Add labels: She clicks the chart title and types 'Pets in Our Class', and sets the vertical axis title to 'Number of children'. Now anyone can read what the bars mean without asking.
Step 6, Read the chart: The Dog bar is tallest at 9 and the Bird bar is shortest at 3. Dog beats Bird by 9 minus 3, which is 6. Sara writes under the chart: 'Dogs are the most popular pet.'
Your turn: 20 children voted for fruit: Apple 7, Banana 5, Mango 8. Total and chart? Model answer: =SUM(B2:B4) gives 20; column chart of A1:B4; the Mango bar is tallest at 8, Banana shortest at 5.

Step 1, Meet the message: In the class chat Noura sees: 'You won a free tablet! Click this link and type your home address and your password.' It comes from someone she does not know, and she feels a little excited and a little unsure.

Step 2, Spot the warning signs: She lists three signs. It promises a free prize, it asks for private details, and the sender is a stranger. A real prize would never ask for a password. That makes this message unsafe.

Step 3, Stop and do not click: Noura keeps the link untouched and types no address or password. Clicking can lead to a fake page. Doing nothing is the safest first action, so she stops before anything else.

Step 4, Tell a trusted adult: She shows her teacher the message and says, 'I think this is not safe.' Her teacher thanks her, helps report it in the app and blocks the sender. Telling an adult is a strong choice.

Step 5, Respectful behaviour: Later a classmate posts a joke about Hadi's drawing. Noura writes, 'I like the colours in your drawing, Hadi,' and does not join the joke. Kind words online follow the same rules as face to face.
Step 6, Check: Noura keeps her password private, did not share her address, reported the unsafe message and spoke kindly. Four good actions. The rule is to think before you click and before you post.

Your turn: A stranger says, 'Send me your photo and school name to win a game.' What do you do? Model answer: do not reply, tell a trusted adult, block the sender, because photos and school names are private details.
Step 1, The scene: At break, Yousef falls and scrapes his knee. He sits on the ground, holds his knee and is crying quietly. Other children walk past because they are busy playing.
Step 2, Notice: Reem stops and looks at Yousef's face. She sees tears and a painful knee. Compassion starts by noticing that someone hurts, and then feeling that you want to help.
Step 3, Choices: Reem could walk on, laugh, call him names, or help. She thinks, 'If I fell, I would want someone to help me.' She picks the choice that cares about his feelings and safety.

Step 4, Help in words and action: She kneels and says gently, 'Are you okay? I will get a teacher.' She stays with him and asks a friend, Omar, to run to the staff room. Words and actions both matter.

Step 5, Result: The teacher arrives in two minutes, cleans the knee and puts on a plaster. Yousef stops crying and says, 'Thank you for staying with me.' Reem did not fix the knee herself, but she got the right help.

Step 6, Sad but not hurt: Another day Yousef is sad because his friend moved away. Reem sits with him and says, 'That sounds hard. I am here.' She listens and does not rush him to cheer up. Compassion includes listening.

Your turn: A classmate drops her lunch and starts to cry. How do you help? Model answer: notice her, say 'That is sad, I am here', ask if she wants help, offer to tell a teacher, and invite her to share your food if allowed.

Step 1, Plan the report: Rashid writes a one-page report on 'Water at School'. Structure: a title, two headings called 'How We Use Water' and 'How We Can Save It', one picture of a tap, and a small table of daily use.

Step 2, Apply styles: He types the title and sets it to Title style, then selects each heading line and applies Heading 1. Using styles rather than changing size by hand lets the program keep headings consistent and build a contents list later.

Step 3, Insert a table: Under the first heading he clicks Insert, Table, and chooses 3 columns by 4 rows. Row 1 holds Place, Litres, Times; rows 2 to 4 hold Sink 10 2, Toilet 6 3, Garden 20 1. The table has 4 rows including the header.

Step 4, Check the total: Rashid works out the daily litres: sink 10 times 2 is 20, toilet 6 times 3 is 18, garden 20 times 1 is 20. The total is 20 plus 18 plus 20, so 58 litres, which he types under the table.

Step 5, Insert the picture and caption: He inserts tap.png beside the second heading, sets text wrapping to Square, shrinks it to a quarter page width, and adds the caption 'Turn off the tap'. Alt text says 'A running tap'.

Step 6, Slide version: He makes one summary slide titled 'Save 58 Litres?' with three bullets: Fix leaks, Turn off taps, Water plants early. Then he saves the report as 'water-report' and the slides as 'water-slides'.

Your turn: Add a table of 3 rows for daily steps (Mon 4000, Tue 5000, Wed 6000). Total? Model answer: Insert Table, 2 columns by 4 rows with a header row; total is 4000 plus 5000 plus 6000, which is 15000 steps.
Step 1, Enter data: Lubna records pocket money saved each day: Monday 5, Tuesday 8, Wednesday 6, Thursday 7, Friday 9. She puts days in A2:A6 and amounts in B2:B6, with headers in row 1.
Step 2, SUM: In B7 she types =SUM(B2:B6). The result is 35, because 5 plus 8 is 13, 13 plus 6 is 19, 19 plus 7 is 26, and 26 plus 9 is 35. A formula starts with an equals sign.
Step 3, AVERAGE: In B8 she types =AVERAGE(B2:B6) and gets 7, since 35 divided by 5 days is 7. She also types =MAX(B2:B6) in B9 and gets 9, and =MIN(B2:B6) in B10 and gets 5.
Step 4, Choose chart: She wants to compare amounts across 5 separate days, so she picks a column chart of A1:B6. A pie chart would be wrong because the days are not parts of one whole choice.

Step 5, Edit and read: She titles the chart 'Savings per Day', labels the vertical axis 'Amount saved', and notes Friday is the tallest bar at 9 while Monday is the shortest at 5. Friday minus Monday is 4.

Step 6, Change a number: She changes Wednesday from 6 to 10. The sum becomes 39 and the average becomes 7.8 because 39 divided by 5 is 7.8. The chart bar for Wednesday grows by itself, which shows formulas update automatically.

Your turn: Rainfall in mm for Jan to Apr is 20, 15, 10, 5. Find the sum, average and chart type. Model answer: sum is 50, average is 12.5, and a line chart suits a change over time, showing a steady fall.

Step 1, The task: Hind researches 'How tall is the tallest tree?' She finds two pages. One is from a university science department, with an author name and a date. The other is a pop-up filled page with no author and loud claims.

Step 2, Check the source: She asks four questions. Who wrote it, when, why, and can I find the same fact elsewhere? Page one answers all four. Page two shows no author, no date and tries to sell something, so she trusts it less.

Step 3, Check the address: She looks at the address bar. Page one ends in a school or university style address and begins with https and a padlock sign. The padlock shows a secure connection, but it does not prove the facts are right.

Step 4, Cross-check: She finds the same height in two more trusted pages: a science museum article and a forestry encyclopedia. Three trustworthy sources agree, so she is confident. One source alone is not enough.

Step 5, Give credit: She writes the fact in her own words, 'The tallest living trees reach over 110 metres,' and adds a source line: author, page title, website name, and date visited. Copying words without credit is not honest.
Step 6, Safe use: While searching she closes a pop-up that asks for her name and email, and she tells her teacher. Only the school's trusted site needed her login. She keeps personal details private.

Your turn: A blog with no author claims a new fruit cures all illness. How do you check it? Model answer: no author or date and an unlikely claim means checking trusted health sources, and if none agree, do not trust it.

Step 1, School case: During a spelling test Noor notices her friend Dana has a small paper with the answers hidden under her desk. Noor is sitting next to her. Her heart beats fast because she must decide what to do.

Step 2, Define integrity: Integrity means doing the right thing even when no one is checking. Noor knows cheating is unfair to children who studied. She thinks of the 10 children who spent a week learning the words.

Step 3, Options: Noor can say nothing, copy the answers too, or speak up kindly. She weighs them. Copying is dishonest. Saying nothing lets unfairness continue. Speaking up carries a small risk, but is honest.
Step 4, Act: After the test, Noor says to Dana quietly, 'I saw the paper. It is not fair to others. Please tell the teacher.' Dana is upset but later tells the teacher, who gives her a retest.

Step 5, Sports case: In a race, Karim reaches the line second, but the referee did not see that the winner stepped out of his lane. Integrity here means Karim says, 'He left his lane,' instead of accepting a medal he did not earn.

Step 6, Why it matters: Honest results mean a score or medal is true. After telling the truth, Noor and Karim feel proud and others trust them. Integrity is a habit built from many small honest choices.

Your turn: Your team wins a game, but you know the scorer gave you one point too many. What do you do? Model answer: tell the scorer so the score is correct, because an honest result is worth more than an unfair point.
Step 1, The task: Hamda leads a group of 5 children to build a recycling display for the corridor. They have 40 minutes and four jobs: collect items, sort them, make labels, and build the stand.

Step 2, Listen first: Hamda asks each member what they would like to do and what they are good at. Fatma likes writing, Zayed likes building, Sama and Ali like sorting, and Hamda herself offers to collect and check.
Step 3, Assign fair roles: Hamda puts Hamda and Ali on collecting, Sama on sorting, Fatma on labels, and Zayed on the stand. Everyone has a clear job, and nobody has two jobs while another has none.

Step 4, Plan time: She sets the plan: collect 10 minutes, sort 10, labels 10, stand 10. That is 10 times 4, which is 40 minutes. Sorting and labels run together in 10 minutes if they start after collection.

Step 5, Solve a problem: Zayed is slow because the stand needs two pairs of hands. Hamda moves Ali to help after collection, and says, 'Thank you, Ali.' A leader adjusts the plan instead of blaming a person.

Step 6, Review: The display is finished in 38 minutes. Hamda asks, 'What went well? What could we change?' Members say roles were clear, and next time start labels earlier. A leader serves the team and shares the credit.

Your turn: Lead 4 children making a class newspaper with four jobs in 20 minutes. Model answer: ask strengths, give one job each (headline, story, picture, layout), 5 minutes each, check at 10 minutes, and thank everyone.

Step 1, Name a global issue: Maha learns that plastic waste reaches the sea around the world. It is a global issue because it affects many countries at the same time. She writes the issue clearly: too much plastic waste in oceans.

Step 2, Local link: She asks, 'Where does plastic waste start near me?' She notices that single-use plastic bottles in the school bins are thrown away every day. The global problem connects to a local habit.
Step 3, Count for evidence: Over 5 school days Maha counts bottles in the class bin: 12, 9, 15, 10, 14. The sum is 12 plus 9 plus 15 plus 10 plus 14, which is 60 bottles in one week for one class.

Step 4, Choose a local action: She proposes that each child brings a reusable bottle. If 60 bottles a week stop, over 4 weeks that is 60 times 4, or 240 fewer bottles in the bin. The goal is clear and countable.

Step 5, Take action: Maha writes a short poster saying, 'Refill, do not waste,' puts it by the water fountain, and asks the teacher to allow a refill point. Her action is small but is aimed at the real cause.

Step 6, Reflect honestly: One class cannot clean the sea, but cutting waste is a real contribution and teaches others. A global citizen thinks about people far away and acts in their own neighbourhood. After 4 weeks she recounts the bottles.

Your turn: Name a global issue about water and one local action. Model answer: the issue is that many places lack clean water, and a local action is turning off taps and fixing a dripping school tap, measured in litres saved.

Step 1, Plan: Saif prepares a report on class reading for four weeks. He needs a table in a word processor, a chart from a spreadsheet, and three slides. First he collects the numbers: minutes read per week.
Step 2, Enter data: In the spreadsheet he types Week 1 to Week 4 in A2:A5, and minutes 120, 150, 180, 210 in B2:B5. Headers in row 1 are Week and Minutes. The increase each week is 30 minutes.
Step 3, Formulas: In B6 he types =SUM(B2:B5) and gets 660 because 120 plus 150 is 270, plus 180 is 450, plus 210 is 660. In B7 he types =AVERAGE(B2:B5) and gets 165, since 660 divided by 4 is 165.
Step 4, Chart: He selects A1:B5 and inserts a line chart, because the numbers change over time. The line rises steadily from 120 to 210. He adds the title 'Reading Minutes per Week' and axis labels.

Step 5, Report page: In the word processor he adds a table, 5 rows by 2 columns, copying the weeks and minutes, pastes the chart under it, and writes, 'Reading grew by 30 minutes each week, to a total of 660 minutes.'

Step 6, Slides: Slide 1 is the title. Slide 2 holds the chart with one sentence, 'Average 165 minutes'. Slide 3 gives one goal: 240 minutes by Week 6, which is 210 plus 30 plus 30. He saves all three files with clear names.

Your turn: Steps walked: Mon 3000, Tue 4000, Wed 5000, Thu 6000. Total, average and chart? Model answer: total 18000, average 4500, a line chart of the four days, and a one-sentence finding that steps rose by 1000 each day.

Step 1, The situation: Alia receives a message from a classmate in a group chat: 'Send me your login code and then I'll do your homework.' Another child posts an unkind photo of a friend, with the caption 'Look at this'.

Step 2, Privacy rule: Alia knows a login code or password is private. She never shares it, even with a friend, because anyone with it can act as her. The rule covers passwords, codes, home address and phone number.

Step 3, Reply respectfully and firmly: She writes, 'No thanks, my codes are private. I will help you with the homework if you want.' She says no politely and offers a safe alternative, so the friendship is not harmed.

Step 4, The unkind photo: Alia does not share or like it. She messages the poster, 'Please delete that, it could hurt her.' She screenshots it, tells her teacher, and checks on the friend. Sharing would spread the harm.

Step 5, Strengthen settings: At home she checks that her account is set to private, uses a password of at least 12 characters mixing words, numbers and symbols, and turns on a second step for sign-in.
Step 6, Review: Her actions followed three ideas. Keep private data private, treat others with respect, and report harm to a trusted adult. If she were unsure, she would pause and ask before posting.

Your turn: A stranger online asks for your school name and photo. Respond using the rules. Model answer: do not send, block and report, tell an adult, because both are private information that could identify you.

Step 1, Find a need: Grade 6 notices that the library has many books on the floor and shelves in a mess. Layla proposes a service project: tidy and label the picture book shelf, which is used by younger children.

Step 2, Set a measurable aim: The team counts 120 books and 6 shelves. The aim is to sort all 120 books by 6 colour labels, 20 books per shelf. 6 shelves times 20 books gives 120, so the plan matches the number.

Step 3, Plan roles and time: 6 volunteers, one shelf each. Each volunteer sorts 20 books, which takes about 20 minutes. All 6 work at once, so the job takes about 20 minutes, not 120 minutes. Layla keeps a checklist.

Step 4, Get permission: Layla asks the librarian, 'May we tidy the picture books on Thursday at break?' She agrees and gives them a trolley. Service in school needs the permission of the adults in charge.

Step 5, Do the service: On Thursday each volunteer sorts a shelf, ticks the checklist and checks labels. At the end the team counts 120 books on 6 shelves with 20 each. The job is complete and the area is clean.

Step 6, Review: The librarian thanks them and a Grade 1 child finds a book easily. The team notes what to improve: start labels first. Service is about helping others, not about praise, and a review makes the next project better.

Your turn: Plan a one-hour service project to clean the school garden with 8 children. Model answer: assign 4 jobs (weeding, watering, litter, tools) in pairs, 15 minutes each rotation = 60 minutes, and ask the gardener first.

Step 1, Set up files: Yara creates a folder called camel-site and opens a plain text editor. She saves a new file as index.html inside it. The .html ending tells the browser that this file is a web page.

Step 2, Basic skeleton: She types <!DOCTYPE html>, then <html>, <head><title>My Camel Page</title></head>, then <body> and </body></html>. The title shows on the browser tab, and everything visible goes between the body tags.

Step 3, Heading and paragraph: Inside body she types

Camels

and

Camels live in the desert and can go days without water.

. In the browser she sees a large bold heading and one line of normal text below it.
Step 4, Image: She copies camel.jpg into the folder and types . The browser shows the picture, and the alt text is read by screen readers and appears if the image fails to load.

Step 5, Link: She types More camel facts. Clicking the blue underlined words opens facts.html, which she creates with

Facts

and

Camels have two humps or one.

. A relative link works because both files are in one folder.

Step 6, Test and fix: She saves and refreshes. The image is missing, so she checks the file name and finds she typed Camel.jpg with a capital C. She changes it to camel.jpg, saves, refreshes, and the picture appears.

Your turn: Make a page with the title 'My Dates', a heading, a paragraph and a link to about.html. Model answer: My Dates,

Dates

,

Sweet fruit.

, About, all inside the body, saved as index.html.

Step 1, Build the table: Faisal sets up a table with fields Name, Class and Score and five records: Ali 7A 82, Bana 7B 91, Cyrus 7A 76, Dina 7B 88, Eman 7A 91. Each row is one record and each column is one field.
Step 2, Sort ascending: He sorts by Score from lowest to highest. The order becomes Cyrus 76, Ali 82, Dina 88, Bana 91, Eman 91. Bana and Eman tie at 91, so they keep their original relative order.
Step 3, Sort descending: He changes the sort to highest first. Now Bana 91, Eman 91, Dina 88, Ali 82, Cyrus 76. The top of the table shows the best scores, which is useful for a quick ranking.
Step 4, Filter by class: He filters Class equals 7A. Only 3 records show: Ali, Cyrus and Eman. The other 2 records, Bana and Dina, are hidden but not deleted. Clearing the filter shows all 5 again.
Step 5, Filter by number: He filters Score greater than or equal to 85. This shows Bana 91, Dina 88 and Eman 91, which is 3 records. Ali at 82 and Cyrus at 76 do not meet the rule.

Step 6, Combine filters: He applies Class equals 7A and Score at least 85 together. Only Eman remains, because Eman is the one record that passes both conditions. Two conditions together are stricter than either alone.

Your turn: Table of books: Sand Tales Story 120, Stars Science 200, Boats Science 90, Moon Story 150 pages. Sort by pages up and filter Science. Model answer: Boats 90, Sand Tales 120, Moon 150, Stars 200; Science filter shows Stars and Boats, 2 records.

Step 1, Define: Noor's digital footprint is every trace she leaves online: posts, photos she shared, comments, accounts, and also what others post about her. Some traces she chose on purpose, like a profile picture, and some are collected from her activity.
Step 2, Audit: She searches for her own name and lists what she finds: 4 public photos, 1 school quiz result, 2 comments on a game forum, and 1 old account she forgot. That is 8 items in total.

Step 3, Sort the items: She marks each item as keep, change or remove. Quiz result keep; 2 comments change, because one uses her full name; 4 photos, 1 shows her school uniform with the school name, so that goes to remove; the old account is removed.

Step 4, Manage: She sets the photo album to friends only, deletes the old account and its posts, and edits the forum name from her real name to a nickname. Items visible to the public drop from 8 to 3, the quiz result and the 2 comments.

Step 5, Think before posting: Before posting a holiday picture she asks, 'Would I be fine if my teacher, grandmother and a stranger saw this in five years?' She also leaves out the location. Posts can be copied and stay long after deletion.

Step 6, Review: Her new footprint shows safe, positive items such as her art competition result. She sets a reminder to check privacy settings every term. Managing a footprint is ongoing, not a one-time job.

Your turn: Audit shows 6 public items, 2 reveal your address. What do you do? Model answer: remove or hide the 2 address items first, set the rest to friends only, and check again; public items drop from 6 to 4 or fewer.

Step 1, The idea: Trust grows slowly through small acts that match your words, like deposits in a jar. Broken promises take out far more than a kept promise puts in. Salman wants to be trusted by his new football team.

Step 2, Small choice one: Salman says he will bring the team ball on Thursday. On Wednesday night he is tired and the ball is in the garden. He puts it in his bag anyway. He keeps a small promise even when no one would check.

Step 3, Small choice two: On Thursday he is late because of a school bus delay. He texts the captain, 'I will be 10 minutes late, start without me.' Telling the truth early is better than showing up without any explanation.

Step 4, A tempting shortcut: His teammate Rami says, 'Say you were on time, the coach will not know.' Salman says, 'I would prefer to tell the truth.' He tells the coach, who says thanks for letting him know.

Step 5, Count the effect: Over 5 weeks, Salman keeps 5 out of 5 promises. By week 5 the captain gives him the job of looking after the equipment. Trust led to more responsibility, which takes time and cannot be rushed.

Step 6, Reasoning: Choosing actions that build trust means asking, 'Will I still be proud of this choice later?' A single lie could hurt several weeks of work. Being honest sometimes costs a little now but protects long-term trust.

Your turn: You promised a friend to keep a secret, but you were tempted to tell. What builds trust? Model answer: keep it unless someone is in danger, and if safety is at stake, tell a trusted adult and explain why to your friend.

Step 1, Situation: In the corridor, three classmates laugh at Tariq's accent as he reads aloud. Maha sees his face go red. She feels afraid to speak because the three children are popular and she might be teased.

Step 2, Name the value: Maha thinks about fairness and respect. Courage does not mean having no fear; it means acting rightly while afraid. She decides the unkind teasing is wrong and she must not be silent.

Step 3, Options: She can stay silent, join the laughing, tell a teacher later, or speak up now. She weighs risk. Joining is wrong. Silence helps the teasing continue. Speaking up now plus telling a teacher is the strongest, safest combination.

Step 4, Speak calmly: Maha steps beside Tariq and says, 'That's not funny. Everyone has an accent. Let him read.' She speaks in a steady voice with no insults, so she is firm without starting a fight.

Step 5, Follow up: After class she tells Tariq, 'I liked your reading.' She also reports the incident to the teacher, who speaks to the three children. One of them, Kamal, apologises to Tariq the next day.

Step 6, Reflect: Maha's courage was small but real. She would have regretted silence. Standing up works best when it is calm, includes the target of the unkindness, and uses an adult for help when the situation is bigger than one student.

Your turn: A friend is excluded from a game on purpose. What courageous step could you take? Model answer: say 'Let her join our team', invite her in, and if the group refuses, play with her and tell a teacher.

Step 1, The message: In a group chat, Reem posts a photo of Nada's drawing with the words 'This looks like a potato.' Several children add laughing faces. Nada reads it and goes quiet, then types, 'Why would you do that?'
Step 2, Pause: Noura sees it and does not rush. She thinks, 'How would Nada feel, and what can I do that helps?' Before replying, she waits a minute. Pausing stops her from adding fuel to the fire.

Step 3, Reply kindly to the group: Noura writes, 'That was unkind. Nada worked hard on it, and I like the colours.' She does not insult Reem. She states what is wrong and adds one honest, true compliment.

Step 4, Reach Nada privately: Noura messages Nada alone, 'I'm sorry that happened. Your drawing is good. Want to sit together at break?' Offline kindness backs up the online words, so Nada does not feel alone.
Step 5, Report: She screenshots the chat and shows the teacher, because unkind messages that humiliate someone should be reported. She also does not forward the photo, so it spreads no further.

Step 6, Result: The next day Reem apologises to Nada in person and deletes the message. The group chat gets a rule: kind words only. Responding kindly means calm words, support for the hurt person and using an adult when needed.

Your turn: Someone writes 'You are so slow' in the class chat about Omar's run. Respond kindly. Model answer: reply 'He tried his best, well done Omar', message Omar privately to check he is fine, and report it if it continues.

Step 1, The decision: Class 7A has 28 students and must pick one trip: Museum, Park or Science Centre. The class agrees to decide fairly, with every voice heard, using a vote after a short discussion.

Step 2, Discuss fairly: Each student gets one minute to speak, with no interruptions. Lina speaks for the museum, Hamad for the park, Rashid for the science centre. Listening before voting is part of fair participation.
Step 3, First vote: A secret paper ballot gives Museum 11, Park 9, Science Centre 8. Check: 11 plus 9 plus 8 is 28, so every student voted once. A majority needs more than 14, so nobody has one yet.

Step 4, Run-off: The class holds a second vote between the top two, Museum and Park. The 8 Science Centre voters now choose: 5 vote Museum and 3 vote Park. Museum has 11 plus 5, which is 16; Park has 9 plus 3, which is 12.

Step 5, Accept the result: 16 plus 12 is 28, and 16 is more than half of 28. Museum wins. Park supporters feel disappointed but accept it, because the process was fair, and the teacher plans a future park picnic.

Step 6, Reflect: A good citizen takes part, listens, votes honestly and respects the outcome. Minority views are heard, and the class tries to include the Park idea later, so the decision serves everyone as far as possible.

Your turn: 20 students choose between 3 games with votes 8, 7, 5. Is there a majority? What next? Model answer: majority needs more than 10, so no; hold a run-off between 8 and 7 games, and the 5 voters choose again.

Step 1, Create a table: Hadi opens a database tool and types: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, grade INTEGER, score INTEGER); The tool replies that the table was created, with four columns and no rows yet.
Step 2, Insert data: He types INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Ali',8,72),(2,'Bana',8,91),(3,'Cyrus',8,65),(4,'Dina',8,88); The tool reports 4 rows added. Text values are in quotes, numbers are not.
Step 3, Select all: SELECT * FROM students; shows all 4 rows and 4 columns. The star means every column. Hadi checks the output matches what he typed, which verifies the insert.
Step 4, Filter and order: SELECT name, score FROM students WHERE score >= 80 ORDER BY score DESC; returns two rows: Bana 91 first, then Dina 88. Ali at 72 and Cyrus at 65 fail the WHERE test.
Step 5, Aggregate: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; returns 4. SELECT AVG(score) FROM students; returns 79.0 because 72 plus 91 plus 65 plus 88 is 316, and 316 divided by 4 is 79.
Step 6, Update and check: UPDATE students SET score = 70 WHERE id = 3; changes Cyrus from 65 to 70. Running AVG again gives 80.25, since the total is now 321 and 321 divided by 4 is 80.25.

Your turn: Table books(id, title, pages) with (1,'Sea',120),(2,'Sky',200),(3,'Sand',80). List books over 100 pages shortest first, and give the count. Model answer: SELECT title, pages FROM books WHERE pages > 100 ORDER BY pages ASC; gives Sea 120, Sky 200; COUNT(*) is 3.
Step 1, Plan the site: Aya builds a 2-page site for a class garden club: index.html (home) and about.html (members), plus one shared style.css. Keeping all three in one folder makes links simple.

Step 2, Shared navigation: In both pages she puts
Home About
inside the body. Clicking Home or About now moves between the pages from either one.
Step 3, Link the stylesheet: In the head of both pages she adds <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">. Without this line the CSS file would be ignored, so every page that wants the style needs it.

Step 4, Write CSS: In style.css she writes body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; background-color: #f4f4f4; } and h1 { color: #036; } and nav a { margin-right: 12px; color: #0a6; }. Each rule has a selector and property: value; pairs.

Step 5, Check both pages: She refreshes index.html and about.html. Both have a light grey background, dark blue headings, and green links spaced 12 pixels apart. One change in style.css affects both pages, which saves time.

Step 6, Fix an error: The About page is not styled because she wrote href="styles.css" with an extra s. She changes it to style.css, refreshes, and the style appears. Matching the exact file name is vital.

Your turn: Add a third page contact.html with the same style and nav. Model answer: copy the head including <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">, add a Contact link in the nav of all 3 pages, and check each page shows the grey background.

Step 1, The task: Zain asks an AI tool, 'What is 15 percent of 240?' The tool replies, '15 percent of 240 is 34.' Zain remembers that AI tools can sound confident but still be wrong, so he plans to check.

Step 2, Check by calculation: He works it out himself. 10 percent of 240 is 24 and 5 percent is 12, so 15 percent is 24 plus 12, which is 36. The tool was wrong by 2. Only the calculation can prove the correct answer.

Step 3, Ask it to show reasoning: Zain writes, 'Show your steps.' The tool now says 240 times 0.15 equals 36. A second try with working gives the right result, but he does not trust it until he has also checked it by hand.

Step 4, Check a source claim: The tool says a book called 'The Desert Rain' by a named author proves a fact. Zain searches the school library catalogue and finds no such book. He treats this as an invented source and does not cite it.

Step 5, Protect privacy: Zain was about to paste his full name, home address and a class photo into the tool. He stops, because anything typed may be stored. He removes the personal details and asks only about the maths.

Step 6, Use honestly: His homework is to write about deserts. He uses the AI for ideas, writes the answer in his own words, checks two facts in a trusted encyclopedia, and tells his teacher he used AI for ideas.

Your turn: An AI says the capital of a country is a city you doubt. What do you do? Model answer: check a trusted atlas or government site, trust the match with two reliable sources, and note that the AI was unreliable.

Step 1, Situation: Waleed finds a tablet in the corridor with a lock screen photo of a younger child and a name label reading 'Hamad G5'. Nobody else is nearby. He wonders whether to keep it, ignore it or return it.

Step 2, Framework: He uses four questions. Who is affected? What are my options? What are the likely results of each? Which option is honest, fair and caring? Writing the answers helps him think clearly instead of reacting.
Step 3, Who and options: Affected people are Hamad, Hamad's family, Waleed and the school. Options are: keep it, leave it where it is, return it to the office, or find Hamad. Four options are listed.

Step 4, Results: Keeping it harms Hamad and is dishonest. Leaving it risks it being lost. Taking it to the office is safe, honest and quick. Finding Hamad directly could work, but the office can check and avoid mix-ups.
Step 5, Decide: Waleed takes the tablet to the front office, says where he found it, and gives the name on the label. The staff contact Hamad's class teacher. The choice is honest, fair and caring.

Step 6, Review: Later Hamad says thank you. Waleed notes the framework slowed him down just enough to choose well. If the choice were harder, such as being asked to keep it secret, he would talk to a trusted adult.

Your turn: You see a friend copy another student's project and hand it in. Use the four questions. Model answer: affected are the owner, friend, teacher and you; options include silence, talking to the friend, telling the teacher; best is asking your friend to fix it, then reporting if not.

Step 1, Situation: At lunch, Ismail's group says, 'We are skipping the last lesson, come with us.' Six friends are going. Ismail does not want to skip because there is a test review, yet he fears being called boring.

Step 2, Spot the pressure: He notices three signs: the group is all agreeing, someone is calling him names if he refuses, and the choice is not his own. Peer pressure is when others push you to act against your own values.

Step 3, Options: Ismail can say yes, say no plainly, say no with an alternative, or walk away. He thinks about what he wants and what might happen: missing the review, getting a detention, or losing some friends.

Step 4, Say no with a line: He says calmly, 'No, I am going to class. I'll see you after school for football.' He uses a short, steady voice, keeps his word choice simple, and offers a different shared plan.

Step 5, Handle a push back: A friend says, 'Come on, don't be a baby.' Ismail answers, 'It's my choice,' and walks to class. He repeats the same sentence and does not argue, because arguing gives the pressure more power.

Step 6, Result and support: Two friends later admit they wished they had stayed. Ismail tells his counsellor about it to be safe. Tools for pressure are: say no, give a reason or alternative, leave, find an ally and tell an adult.
Your turn: Friends dare you to post a rude joke about a teacher. Respond. Model answer: say 'No, I'm not posting that', suggest another activity, walk away, and tell an adult if they keep pushing.

Step 1, Choose the act: Grade 8 wants to thank the 12 school support staff: cleaners, guards, canteen and bus helpers. Dalal proposes handwritten thank-you notes and a tidy-up of the staff room. Gratitude means noticing and valuing what others do for us.
Step 2, Plan: There are 4 classes with 24 students each, so 96 students. They agree that every student writes 1 note, so that is 96 notes. 96 divided by 12 staff is 8 notes per person.

Step 3, Set roles: Each class picks a lead, collects notes in a box and sorts them into 12 envelopes, 8 notes each. Dalal checks the count: 12 envelopes times 8 notes is 96, matching the number of students.

Step 4, Do the act: On Thursday the leads hand out envelopes. Notes include specific details, like 'Thank you for opening the gate early every morning.' Specific thanks show real attention, unlike a general 'thank you'.

Step 5, Staff room help: Six volunteers wipe tables and recycle papers in 15 minutes after asking permission. They leave without asking for praise. Service is for the other person, not for being seen.

Step 6, Review: Dalal asks the staff and students what went well. A guard says he kept his note. Next time they plan a thank-you for the bus team. Reviewing improves the next act, and honest feelings are better than claiming huge results.

Your turn: Plan a thank-you act for 5 teachers from 30 students. Model answer: each student writes 1 note, 30 divided by 5 is 6 notes per teacher, 5 envelopes of 6, give them on a set day, then review.

Step 1, Variables and decisions: Sami types marks = 72 then if marks >= 90: print('A') elif marks >= 70: print('B') else: print('C'), with each print line indented four spaces. Python checks conditions top to bottom, and 72 fails the first test but passes the second.

Step 2, Run it: The output is B. If he changes marks to 95 the first condition is true and A prints; the elif and else parts are skipped. Only the first true branch runs, which is why the order of conditions matters.
Step 3, A for loop: He types for i in range(1, 4): print(i * i). range(1, 4) gives 1, 2, 3 because the end value 4 is not included. The program prints 1, then 4, then 9, one per line.

Step 4, A while loop: He types total = 0, n = 1, then while n <= 5: total = total + n and n = n + 1 on indented lines, then print(total). Adding 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5 gives 15, so 15 is printed.

Step 5, Debug: He forgets n = n + 1 and the loop never ends because n stays 1. He stops the program with Ctrl+C, adds the missing line, and the loop ends after 5 passes. A while loop must change something that eventually makes its condition false.

Step 6, Input: He adds age = int(input('Age? ')). Typing 14 gives the number 14, because int converts the text to a whole number. Then print(age + 1) outputs 15. Without int, adding 1 to text would cause an error.

Your turn: Print the first five even numbers using a loop, and their total. Model answer: total = 0, for i in range(1, 6): print(i * 2), total = total + i * 2, then print(total). Output 2 4 6 8 10 and then 30.

Step 1, Decompose: Huda must plan a class bake sale. She breaks it into smaller parts: choose items, count how many of each, make a price-free sign, set up the stall, and clean up. Five small tasks are easier than one big one.

Step 2, Find patterns: Each baker follows the same pattern: bring item, tell the team, place on the table. She notices she can write this once and reuse it for all 8 bakers. Spotting repeated steps is pattern recognition.

Step 3, Abstract: Huda ignores detail like the colour of the tablecloth and keeps what matters: item name and number brought. A table with two columns, Item and Count, represents the real situation in a simple model.

Step 4, Algorithm to find the largest count: List is 12, 7, 19, 4. Steps: set largest to the first number; look at each next number; if it is bigger than largest, replace largest; when no numbers remain, report largest.

Step 5, Trace it: Start largest 12. Compare 7: not bigger. Compare 19: bigger, so largest becomes 19. Compare 4: not bigger. No numbers remain, so the answer is 19. Tracing by hand proves the algorithm before coding it.

Step 6, Flowchart and test: She draws Start, set largest, a loop with a decision diamond 'Next number > largest?', Yes or No arrows, and End. She tests with 5, 5, 5; the result is 5, correct for equal numbers.

Your turn: Find the smallest number in 8, 3, 11, 5 and trace it. Model answer: start smallest 8; 3 is smaller so smallest 3; 11 not; 5 not; answer 3. Steps mirror the largest algorithm with the comparison reversed.

Step 1, The raw data: Raed's sheet has 7 rows: Ali 72; bana 91; Cyrus blank; Dina 88; Dina 88; Eman 65; Fadi 150. The maximum score is 100, so some entries look wrong. Before analysis the data must be cleaned.

Step 2, Fix format: He makes names consistent by changing bana to Bana and trimming extra spaces. Consistent text means sorting and searching work properly. Visible spaces or capitals can make the same name look different to a computer.
Step 3, Remove duplicates: Dina 88 appears twice, so he deletes one copy. The sheet now has 6 rows. Duplicates would count one student twice and distort totals and averages.

Step 4, Handle missing and impossible values: Cyrus has no score, so he marks it as missing and leaves it out. Fadi 150 is above 100, so he flags it as an error to check with the teacher. Valid rows left: Ali, Bana, Dina, Eman.
Step 5, Sort and summarise: Sorting scores highest first gives Bana 91, Dina 88, Ali 72, Eman 65. The maximum is 91 and the minimum is 65. The sum is 72 plus 91 plus 88 plus 65, which is 316.

Step 6, Average and record: The average is 316 divided by 4, which is 79. He writes a note: 4 valid of 7 original rows; 1 duplicate, 1 missing and 1 impossible. Recording what was removed keeps the analysis honest.
Your turn: Scores 60, 80, blank, 80 (duplicate student), 120. Clean and average. Model answer: remove the duplicate 80, ignore blank, flag 120, leaving 60 and 80; the average is 70.

Step 1, Learn from labelled data: A fruit sorter is given 6 labelled examples. Plums weigh 120, 130 and 140 grams. Apples weigh 180, 190 and 200 grams. The machine looks for a rule that separates the two labels.

Step 2, Learn a rule: The gap lies between 140 and 180. The middle is (140 plus 180) divided by 2, which is 160. The learned rule is: weight below 160 is plum, 160 or above is apple. This is a very simple model.

Step 3, Predict: A new fruit weighs 150 grams, so it is below 160 and the model says plum. A fruit weighing 185 is above 160, so it is called apple. The model has never seen these exact weights before.

Step 4, Test: The tester has 4 new labelled fruits: 135 plum, 175 apple, 145 plum, 195 apple. The model labels 135 plum (right), 175 apple (right), 145 plum (right), 195 apple (right). Accuracy is 4 of 4, which is 100 percent.
Step 5, Where bias comes from: A face unlock tool is trained on 90 photos of one group and 10 of another. It is right 95 percent of the time for the first group and 60 percent for the second group.

Step 6, Compute the hidden gap: Overall accuracy is (90 times 0.95 plus 10 times 0.60) divided by 100, which is (85.5 plus 6) divided by 100, giving 91.5 percent. The good overall number hides a 35 point gap between groups.

Step 1, A function with exception handling: def safe_div(a, b): try: return a / b except ZeroDivisionError: return None. safe_div(10, 2) returns 5.0 and safe_div(5, 0) returns None instead of crashing the program.

Step 2, Test with assert: assert safe_div(10, 2) == 5.0 passes silently. assert safe_div(5, 0) is None also passes. If a test fails, Python raises AssertionError with the line number, so the bug is found quickly.
Step 3, Prepare a file: nums.txt contains three lines: 4, then x, then 6. The goal is to total the valid numbers. The expected answer is 4 plus 6, which is 10, and x should be skipped and reported.

Step 4, Read with handling: def read_total(path): total = 0, then with open(path) as f: for line in f: try: total += int(line) except ValueError: print('skip', line.strip()), then return total. Each int() is guarded by its own try block.

Step 5, Run and check: read_total('nums.txt') prints skip x and returns 10. Because int('4\n') and int('6\n') accept surrounding whitespace, they convert, but int('x') raises ValueError, which is caught, so the loop continues.

Step 6, Missing file: read_total('none.txt') raises FileNotFoundError because open fails. A caller wraps it in try and except FileNotFoundError and prints 'No such file'. Different errors need different handlers, and a bare except would hide mistakes.

Step 1, The layers: A browser request passes through four layers. Application: HTTP data. Transport: TCP splits it into segments with port numbers, such as 443 for secure web traffic. Network: IP adds source and destination addresses. Link: frames move it over one hop.

Step 2, Follow one request: A student opens a page. The browser makes an HTTP request, TCP adds the destination port 443, IP adds the server's address, and the link layer sends the frame to the router. The server reverses the process, so the reply climbs the layers.

Step 3, Subnet: 192.168.1.0/24 has a prefix of 24 bits, leaving 8 host bits. 2 to the power 8 is 256 addresses, and two are reserved, the network and the broadcast, so 254 hosts can be used. The mask is 255.255.255.0.

Step 4, Split into smaller subnets: With /26 there are 6 host bits, so 2 to the power 6 gives 64 addresses and 62 usable hosts. The first subnet is 192.168.1.0 to 192.168.1.63, with hosts .1 to .62, and the next starts at .64. The mask is 255.255.255.192.

Step 5, Encryption example: A Caesar cipher with shift 3 changes CAT to FDW, because C moves to F, A to D and T to W. It is easy to break, so real systems use strong, well-tested algorithms. Never design your own for real data.

Step 6, Password strength: An 8-letter lowercase password has 26 to the power 8, about 208.8 billion possibilities. With 62 characters, upper and lower case letters and digits, 62 to the power 8 is about 218 trillion. Longer, varied passwords are much harder to guess.
Your turn: How many usable hosts in a /28 subnet? Model answer: 32 minus 28 is 4 host bits; 2 to the power 4 is 16 addresses; minus the network and broadcast addresses gives 14 usable hosts.

Step 2, Insert safely: cur.executemany('INSERT INTO marks VALUES (?, ?)', [('Ali', 72), ('Bana', 91), ('Cyrus', 65), ('Dina', 88)]) then con.commit(). Without commit the rows are not saved. Running this twice would add 8 rows, so run it once.

Step 3, Query: cur.execute('SELECT name, score FROM marks WHERE score >= 80 ORDER BY score DESC') then print(cur.fetchall()). Output: [('Bana', 91), ('Dina', 88)]. fetchall returns a list of tuples, one per row.

Step 4, Aggregate: cur.execute('SELECT AVG(score) FROM marks') then print(cur.fetchone()[0]). The output is 79.0 because 72 plus 91 plus 65 plus 88 is 316, and 316 divided by 4 is 79. fetchone returns one tuple.

Step 5, Parameters not string joining: user_name = 'Ali', cur.execute('SELECT score FROM marks WHERE name = ?', (user_name,)) returns [(72,)] with fetchall. The question mark keeps user input as data, which prevents SQL injection from input like x' OR '1'='1.
Step 6, Close: con.close() releases the file. Wrapping work in try and finally ensures the connection closes even after an error. Reopening school.db and running COUNT(*) should still return 4 rows.
